---
title: "Images, Tables, Diagrams and References"
subtitle: "Everything on the page that is not running text"
---

::: {.objectives}
**In this chapter**

- Add an image with a caption and a text alternative, and refer to it in the text
- Build a table and keep it readable
- Draw a simple diagram without a drawing program
- Embed a video responsibly
- Cite a source and get the reference list for free
:::

## Images

Put every image file in the `images/` folder. Then insert it in one of two ways.

- **Visual mode**: *Insert → Figure / Image…*, pick the file, type a caption and
  the *Alt text*, and confirm.
- **Source mode**:

```markdown
![A short caption under the picture](images/placeholder.svg){#fig-demo fig-alt="A dark blue placeholder picture with the words: Your picture goes here."}
```

Here is the result. Click the picture: it opens enlarged, which helps with
screenshots and detailed diagrams.

![A short caption under the picture](images/placeholder.svg){#fig-demo fig-alt="A dark blue placeholder picture with the words: Your picture goes here."}

### Alt text is not optional

The **alt text** is a description of the picture for people who cannot see it:
blind and low-vision learners using a screen reader, and anyone whose image has
not loaded. In the EU, accessibility is also a legal requirement for most
public-sector websites. Write what the picture *shows and why it is there*, in a sentence or
two: "Screenshot of the Build tab with the Render Website button highlighted",
not "screenshot" or "image1".

The caption and the alt text do different jobs. The caption is for everybody and
says what to notice. The alt text stands in for the picture.

### Referring to a picture

Notice the `{#fig-demo}` in the source above. That label lets you point to the
figure by number from anywhere in the chapter: typing `@fig-demo` produces
@fig-demo. The number updates itself if you add a figure before it. Labels for
figures must start with `fig-`, and for tables with `tbl-`.

### Choosing and preparing images

| Situation | Best format |
|---|---|
| Screenshot, diagram, chart | PNG, or SVG for drawings |
| Photograph | JPG |
| Logo or line drawing you can scale | SVG |
: Which file type to use {#tbl-formats}

- **Keep files small.** A photo straight from a phone can be many megabytes and
  makes the course slow to load. Scale it down (a width of about 1600 pixels is
  plenty) before adding it.
- **Do not put text in images.** It cannot be searched, resized or read aloud.
  Put the text in the page and use the image for what only an image can show.
- **Use only images you have the right to use.** Pictures found online are
  usually copyrighted. Use your own, the university's, or material with a clear
  licence, and credit the source in the caption.
- **Never publish anything that identifies a patient** unless you hold explicit
  consent and your institution has approved it. Remember that the finished
  course will be public (Chapter 8).

## Tables

A table shows a comparison, or a list of items each with the same properties. In
Visual mode use **Insert → Table** and type into the cells. In Source mode a table
is drawn with vertical bars:

```markdown
| Tool | Used for | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| RStudio | Writing and building the course | Free |
| GitHub | Publishing the course | Free for public courses |
: The tools in this course {#tbl-tools}
```

The line starting with a colon is the caption, and the label works like a figure's
label: `@tbl-tools` gives @tbl-tools.

| Tool | Used for | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| RStudio | Writing and building the course | Free |
| GitHub | Publishing the course | Free for public courses |
: The tools in this course {#tbl-tools}

Keep tables **small** (rarely more than five columns) and never use a table just
to arrange things on the page. If a table gets wide, it usually wants to be two
tables, or a list.

## Diagrams without a drawing program

For processes and relationships, you can *describe* the diagram in text and let
the website draw it. This is called **Mermaid**. It is ideal for flow charts,
and diagrams stay editable: to change a box, change a word.

Type a block like this:

````markdown
```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-flow
%%| fig-cap: "The working rhythm"
%%| fig-alt: "Three boxes in a row: Edit, Render, Check. An arrow leads from each to the next, and from Check back to Edit."
flowchart LR
    A["Edit"] --> B["Render"]
    B --> C["Check"]
    C --> A
```
````

Each box is `letter["Label"]`, and `-->` draws an arrow between two of them. The
result:

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-flow
%%| fig-cap: "The working rhythm"
%%| fig-alt: "Three boxes in a row: Edit, Render, Check. An arrow leads from each to the next, and from Check back to Edit."
flowchart LR
    A["Edit"] --> B["Render"]
    B --> C["Check"]
    C --> A
```

To colour boxes in the university's palette, add these lines at the end of the
diagram and list the boxes that should get each style:

```markdown
    classDef dark fill:#203151,stroke:#203151,color:#ffffff
    classDef gold fill:#f1a400,stroke:#f1a400,color:#000000
    class A,B dark
    class C gold
```

The first two lines define a style (dark blue with white text; yellow with black
text, as the corporate design allows), the last two apply them. The landing page
of this course uses exactly this.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## When not to use a diagram

If you find yourself fighting the tool to get a complicated picture, draw it in
any program you like, export it as PNG or SVG, and use it as an ordinary image.
Do not spend an afternoon on a diagram.
:::

## Video

A short video can explain a movement or a screen recording better than a page of
text. Use the video shortcode with a web address or a local file:

```markdown
{{{< video media/hand-disinfection.mp4 >}}}
```

Two things to consider before you add one:

- **Where it is hosted matters.** Embedding a video from a public platform makes
  the learner's browser contact that company, which raises data-protection
  questions for a public university. Prefer a video hosted by the university or
  your own project, and ask your data-protection officer what is approved.
- **Provide a transcript or captions.** Learners who cannot hear, and learners
  in a quiet library, need them.

## Citing sources

If you refer to research or guidelines, cite them properly. The template builds
the reference list automatically.

1. **Keep your sources in one file**, `references.bib`. Each source has a short
   *key* of your choosing, for example `roediger2006test`.
2. **Cite in the text** by typing `@` and the key: `[@roediger2006test]` gives
   [@roediger2006test]. To cite two, separate with a semicolon:
   `[@sweller1988cognitive; @mayer2009multimedia]`.
3. **The list appears** wherever the page `references.qmd` says so. You do not
   type it.

You almost never have to write `references.bib` by hand. If you use the
reference manager **Zotero**, export your collection as *BibTeX* and save it over
`references.bib`. In RStudio's Visual mode, **Insert → Citation…** can also look a
source up by its DOI and add it for you.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Cite for the learner, not for show

A good course cites where a claim needs support or where a learner might want to
read further. It does not need a citation after every sentence. Two or three
well-chosen sources per chapter are plenty.
:::

## Check your understanding

::: {.quiz-score}
:::

::: {.question}
Where should the image files for the course be stored?

- [ ] Anywhere; the website finds them
- [x] In the `images/` folder of the project
- [ ] In the `docs/` folder
- [ ] Pasted into a Word document next to the chapter

::: {.feedback}
Keep all pictures in `images/`, so they are in one place and the links in your
chapters stay short and consistent. Never place anything in `docs/`; it is
overwritten at every render.
:::
:::

::: {.question}
Which is the best alt text for a screenshot of the Build tab?

- [ ] Screenshot
- [ ] image1.png
- [x] The Build tab in RStudio, with the Render Website button highlighted
- [ ] Look at the picture above

::: {.feedback}
Alt text should say what the picture shows and why it is there, so that someone
who cannot see it gets the same information.
:::
:::

::: {.question}
You have a 6 MB photograph from a phone camera. What should you do before using it?

- [ ] Nothing; the website compresses it automatically
- [x] Scale it down to about 1600 pixels wide and save it as a JPG
- [ ] Convert it to a table
- [ ] Type the caption into the picture

::: {.feedback}
The website serves the file exactly as it is, so a huge image slows every
learner's page down. Scale it before you add it.
:::
:::

In the text, a citation is written by typing the sign [?]{.fitb answer="@"} followed by the key.
